findings.claim: The decision-making chapter (Ch 6) names stakeholders explicitly as "all the individuals or groups that are affected by an organization (such as customers, employees, shareholders, etc.)" [V]
findings.failure_mode: [V] quotation not carried by the deep ref
findings.evidence: The words are verbatim in source 7970-7971 (Ch 6.1), so the marker fits, but the deep ref has no Ch 6.1 content and no stakeholder definition; the quote was taken from the source at Pass G.
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add to deep Part VI a Ch 6.1 entry: 'Stakeholders are all the individuals or groups that are affected by an organization (such as customers, employees, shareholders, etc.)' [V] (source 7970-7971); the glossary (9047-9048) adds owners, suppliers and community members.

findings.claim: ... and frames stakeholder consideration as central to ethical decision-making.
findings.failure_mode: loosened; not in deep
findings.evidence: Deep 198 (Rest's model) does not mention stakeholders. The source ties stakeholders to decision quality (7969-7971) and to evidence gathering (8616-8617); the ethics passage asks whether options cause harm 'and if so, how much and to whom' (8761). It does not call stakeholder consideration central to ethical decision-making.
findings.fix: correct: ... and treats the effect of a decision on stakeholders as part of judging its quality and its ethics (Ch 6.1, Ch 6.5).

findings.claim: All individuals or groups affected by an organisation, including customers, employees, shareholders, suppliers, regulators, and communities. The list expands by context. (Source: Ch 6.1)
findings.failure_mode: source-supported, absent from deep; one item added
findings.evidence: As D001. Source 7970-7971 and glossary 9047-9048 name customers, employees, shareholders/owners, suppliers and community members; 'regulators' appears in neither.
findings.fix: correct: drop 'regulators'. cycle-to-deep: as D001.

findings.claim: Pooled (...), sequential (...), and reciprocal (...). The type of interdependence determines how much interaction is needed; high reciprocal interdependence requires high integration.
findings.failure_mode: definitions absent from deep; two interaction requirements merged
findings.evidence: Deep 304 names the three types without definitions; source 14374-14410 gives the definitions and says reciprocal interdependence means 'requiring a high degree of interaction'. Deep 304 treats integration as a separate interaction requirement (collaboration despite different goals and time orientations).
findings.fix: correct: ... high reciprocal interdependence requires a high degree of interaction. cycle-to-deep: add the three definitions (source 14393-14410) to deep 304.

findings.claim: decoupling separates groups whose conflict cannot be productively resolved
findings.failure_mode: source-supported, absent from deep
findings.evidence: Deep 304 lists decoupling without a gloss. Source 14601-14606: decoupling is for groups that 'simply don't work together effectively', separating them 'physically or administratively' so tasks are done while interaction is minimised.
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add the decoupling gloss (source 14601-14606) to deep 304.

findings.claim: Collaboration suits high-stakes integrative conflicts; compromise suits time-pressured situations of equal power; accommodation suits situations where the issue matters more to the other side.
findings.failure_mode: source-supported, absent from deep; two conditions merged
findings.evidence: Deep 444-448 give collaborating (integrative solution needed), compromising (goals important but not worth disruption), accommodating (issues matter more to others). Source Table 14.1 (21207-21209) lists 'opponents with equal power' and 'expedient solutions under time pressure' as separate compromising situations.
findings.fix: correct: compromise suits opponents of equal power committed to exclusive goals, or expedient settlements under time pressure. cycle-to-deep: add source Table 14.1 (21195-21240) situations to deep 442-448 (the deep labels them Exhibit 14.4; the source table is Table 14.1).

findings.claim: Strong BATNA holders need not concede; weak BATNA holders should examine whether reaching an agreement is in their interest.
findings.failure_mode: source's condition inverted
findings.evidence: Deep 464 [V] and source 21975-21977: 'the party with the more attractive BATNA gets the better of the deal. If both parties have attractive BATNAs, the best course of action may be not to reach an agreement at all.' Walking away is the option when BATNAs are attractive; a weak BATNA makes agreement more, not less, worth having.
findings.fix: correct: "In general, the party with the more attractive BATNA gets the better of the deal. If both parties have attractive BATNAs, the best course of action may be not to reach an agreement at all" [V] (Ch 14.4).

findings.claim: Four cultural negotiation differences. Direct versus indirect communication, attitudes toward hierarchy, decision-making norms, and accent and fluency. (Source: Ch 10.6 and Ch 14.4)
findings.failure_mode: concept re-labelled; mis-cited chapter
findings.evidence: Deep 328 and source 15710-15711 (Ch 10.6): 'four key cultural differences that can cause destructive conflicts in a team'. Ch 14.4's cross-cultural negotiation content is different (deep 460, 466: stage emphasis; factual/affective/axiomatic styles, Table 14.5). Same pattern as software-business D021/D043.
findings.fix: correct: Four cultural differences that cause conflict in multicultural teams: ... (Source: Ch 10.6). For negotiation, add Ch 14.4's differences in stage emphasis and persuasion style (Table 14.5).

findings.claim: Managers spend the majority of their time with peers across organisational boundaries (47 per cent in Stewart's 1967 study)
findings.failure_mode: figure contradicts the word it supports
findings.evidence: Deep 344 and source 16566-16567: 47% with peers, 41% inside the unit, 12% with superiors. 47% is not a majority; the source says managers spend 'as much time with peers and other people outside of their units as they do with their own subordinates' (16562-16564).
findings.fix: correct: Managers spend about as much time with peers outside their unit as with their own people (47 per cent with peers, 41 per cent within the unit, 12 per cent with superiors, in Stewart's 1967 study) [BT]

findings.claim: Competing (when speed and authority warrant), ... compromising (time-pressured equal-power), avoiding (trivial or symptoms-not-causes) ...
findings.failure_mode: source-supported, absent from deep; one condition added (recurrence of D006)
findings.evidence: Deep 444-448 carry only emergencies/unpopular actions, trivial issues. Source Table 14.1 (21200-21235) supports speed ('quick, decisive action is vital'), equal power and time pressure (separately), and symptomatic issues; 'authority' is not among competing's situations.
findings.fix: correct: Competing (when quick, decisive action is vital or an unpopular action must be implemented) ... compromising (equal power, or time pressure) ... cycle-to-deep: as D006.

findings.claim: Are we applying procedural justice? Even when distributive outcomes disappoint, fair process sustains commitment.
findings.failure_mode: mechanism not in deep
findings.evidence: Deep 239 [AP] (Ch 7.4) defines distributive and procedural justice with the seniority-layoff example only; source 11128-11147 says nothing about commitment. Same finding as software-business D007/D015/D022.
findings.fix: correct: Are we applying procedural justice? People judge the fairness of the process as well as the outcome (Ch 7.4).

findings.claim: Diagnosis: coercive or pure-reward power being used where referent or expert power would have produced commitment.
findings.failure_mode: power-base responses mis-assigned
findings.evidence: Deep 368 (Exhibit 12.5): reward power elicits a measured, tit-for-tat response (not alienation); coercive power produces alienation and resistance; referent power produces identification (not commitment); rationality, expertise and moralistic appeal produce commitment.
findings.fix: correct: Diagnosis: coercive power (alienation, resistance) or reward power (measured, tit-for-tat response) being used where rationality or expertise would have produced commitment (Ch 12.3).

findings.claim: cultural intelligence (head, body, heart) may be needed. Follow-up: sense the emotional and value dimensions; engage the heart as well as the head.
findings.failure_mode: framework applied to the wrong party
findings.evidence: Deep 328: head-body-heart are the cognitive, physical and emotional/motivational components of one's own cultural intelligence. Source 15863-15865: the heart 'deals with a person's own confidence in their ability to adapt' and 'one's own level of emotional commitment and motivation to understand the new culture'. It is not a channel for engaging others' emotions.
findings.fix: correct: ... emotion, identity and values may be operating. Follow-up: sense the emotional and value dimensions; on the engager's side, cultural intelligence means knowing the culture (head), adapting demeanour (body) and committing to adapt (heart) (Ch 10.6).

findings.claim: The source defines stakeholders as "all the individuals or groups ..." [V] and positions stakeholder consideration as central to ethical decision-making (Source: OpenStax, Organizational Behavior, Ch 6.1).
findings.failure_mode: quotation not from the deep ref; ethics claim loosened and cited to Ch 6.1 (recurrence of D001/D002)
findings.evidence: As D001 and D002. The ethics material is Ch 6.5 (deep 198), not Ch 6.1. The protocol requires Worked Example blockquotes to be copied from the deep ref's audited [V] passages.
findings.fix: correct: as D002; cycle-to-deep as D001.

findings.claim: Applying French and Raven's five power bases (Ch 12.3, Ch 13.1): ... operations holds resource power.
findings.failure_mode: a sixth base added to a five-base framework
findings.evidence: Deep 360-366: reward, coercive, referent, expert, legitimate. 'Resource power' belongs to the Salancik-Pfeffer resource-dependence model (deep 424), not French and Raven.
findings.fix: correct: ... operations controls critical resources (Salancik-Pfeffer resource dependence, Ch 13.3).

findings.claim: compromising with payers (time-pressured, equal-power) ... applying all four cultural negotiation differences the source names (Ch 10.6, Ch 14.4).
findings.failure_mode: recurrence of D006 and D008
findings.evidence: As D006 (compromise conditions merged; not in deep) and D008 (the four are Ch 10.6 team-conflict sources, not negotiation differences).
findings.fix: correct: ... applying the four cultural differences the source names as sources of conflict in multicultural teams (Ch 10.6).

findings.claim: The community board raises emotional concerns; the director engages through head, body, and heart (Ch 10.6).
findings.failure_mode: framework applied to the wrong party (recurrence of D013)
findings.evidence: As D013: head-body-heart describe the director's own cultural intelligence, not a method for engaging a board's emotional concerns.
findings.fix: correct: The community board raises emotional concerns; the director acknowledges them directly rather than answering only with data.

findings.claim: all framework citations trace through the deep ref at corpus.commons/demo/references/openstax-organizational-behavior-deep.md.
findings.failure_mode: integrity claim not borne out
findings.evidence: The stakeholder definition (line 133) and the Thomas-mode conditions (line 137) are not in the deep ref (D001, D006).
findings.fix: correct: framework citations trace through the deep ref except the Ch 6.1 stakeholder definition and the Table 14.1 mode conditions, which come from the source and are queued for the deep ref.

findings.claim: The head alone misses the body and heart sources of cultural intelligence; engagements that exclude emotion and values fail in cultures where these are central.
findings.failure_mode: framework applied to the wrong party; outcome claim added
findings.evidence: As D013 for head-body-heart. Deep 466 (Table 14.5) supports cultural differences in persuasion style (factual, affective, axiomatic) but says nothing about such engagements failing.
findings.fix: correct: Pure-rationality engagement with culturally diverse stakeholders. Persuasion styles differ across cultures (factual, affective, axiomatic; Ch 14.4, Table 14.5); facts alone may not persuade a party that leads with feelings or ideals.

findings.claim: Equity theory predicts disengagement when the link between effort, outcome, and reward is unclear
findings.failure_mode: one theory's mechanism given to another
findings.evidence: Deep 231: equity theory compares one's outcome-input ratio with a referent's. Deep 233: the effort-performance-outcome link is expectancy theory's. Same finding as software-business D032.
findings.fix: correct: Expectancy theory predicts weaker motivation when the link between effort, performance and reward is unclear, and equity theory predicts restorative action when people judge their ratio unfair against a referent (Ch 7.3); both apply to internal stakeholders.

findings.claim: Avoiding conflict ... allows substantive disagreements to fester and re-emerge as relationship conflict.
findings.failure_mode: mechanism added
findings.evidence: Deep 190 and source 8386-8414: avoiding a needed conflict lets the problem continue and compound (others copy the behaviour; good employees leave). Nothing says avoided process conflict turns into relationship conflict.
findings.fix: correct: ... allows substantive disagreements to fester and the underlying problem to compound (Ch 6.4).

findings.claim: Procedural justice — fair process — sustains stakeholder commitment even when distributive outcomes disappoint.
findings.failure_mode: mechanism not in deep (recurrence of D011)
findings.evidence: As D011.
findings.fix: correct: Procedural justice: people judge the fairness of the process as well as the outcome; layoffs by seniority are seen as fairer than by supervisors' opinion (Ch 7.4).

findings.claim: AI offers a bottom-up alternative that produces stronger commitment than top-down ratification processes.
findings.failure_mode: comparative outcome claim not in deep
findings.evidence: Deep 536 and 725: AI is abundance-based and bottom-up; 'the more complex the potential change, the greater the need to involve employees'. Source 24819-24909: appreciative conversations shift narratives and 'inspire a shift in the actions that employees initiate'. No comparison of commitment against top-down processes.
findings.fix: correct: AI offers a bottom-up alternative in which participants co-create the vision and design the actions (Ch 16.3).

findings.claim: The deep ref carries 73 `[BT]` markers.
findings.failure_mode: count wrong
findings.evidence: The current deep ref (sha256 a475cbbb..., matching the derived-from-deep header) has 83 [BT] markers (75 '[BT]' plus 8 '[BT, ...]') on 80 lines.
findings.fix: correct: The deep ref carries 83 `[BT]` markers.

findings.claim: The deep ref notes that pedagogical scaffolding ... was excluded; substantive chapter content was covered in full.
findings.failure_mode: coverage overstated
findings.evidence: Deep 396: Ch 12.7-12.8 are 'sections present but not fully covered in the read'.
findings.fix: correct: ... was excluded; the deep ref flags Ch 12.7-12.8 as not fully covered, and all other substantive content was covered.

findings.claim: The deep ref's key stakeholder-engagement claims carry `[V]` markers for direct quotations (e.g., the stakeholder definition from Ch 6.1; the 47-per-cent liaison figure from Ch 11.3; the multicultural conflict sources from Ch 10.6) and `[AP]` markers for the source's paraphrase of French-Raven, Thomas, and BATNA frameworks. ... Where the distillation cites 'Ch N, Section name', the corresponding `[V]` or `[AP]` passage is in the deep ref
findings.failure_mode: integrity note false about the deep ref
findings.evidence: The deep ref has no stakeholder definition (D001). The 47% figure is [BT] (deep 344); the multicultural conflict sources are [BT] (deep 328); French-Raven is unmarked (deep 360); Thomas is [BT] (deep 442); BATNA is [BT] with a separate [V] sentence (deep 464). No [AP] marks any of the three frameworks.
findings.fix: correct: The deep ref carries these frameworks as [BT] (47 per cent figure, multicultural conflict sources, Thomas, BATNA) or unmarked (French-Raven); the BATNA-attractiveness sentence is [V]. The Ch 6.1 stakeholder definition is quoted from the source and is not yet in the deep ref.

notes: Counting: claims_audited counts distinct assertions (relevance sentences, key-concept sub-claims, table rows, pattern and anti-pattern items, worked-example steps, integration rows, borrowed-through items, named limits, integrity-note items); faithful = claims_audited - findings; where one finding covers two sub-claims on one line it counts once (D016). Quote check against the converted source: the stakeholder definition (7970-7971) is word for word but absent from the deep ref (D001). The derived-from-deep sha256 (a475cbbb...) matches the current deep ref. Structural (not graded): the Integration section's nine rows are all frameworks inside this same source (Simon, Thomas, Fisher and Ury, Salancik and Pfeffer, Hofstede and Kluckhohn-Strodtbeck, Katz and Kahn, Adams, Cooperrider, Mintzberg) and link to no other corpus reference, which the protocol's Integration template requires. Judged faithful: 'peers across organisational boundaries' for the 47 per cent figure (the source says peers 'outside of their units' and contacts 'outside the vertical chain of command', 16561-16564); the BATNA analysis in the Worked Example (hypothetical reasoning, not presented as a source finding); 'Fisher, Ury, and Patton' (source endnote 31852 names Bruce Patton). Recurring claims listed at each occurrence: stakeholder definition (D001, D003, D014); Thomas-mode conditions (D006, D010, D016); four cultural differences as negotiation differences (D008, D016); head-body-heart applied to others (D013, D017, D019); procedural justice sustaining commitment (D011, D022). Deep-ref gaps surfaced (cycling candidates): Ch 6.1 stakeholder definition (7970-7971; glossary 9047-9048), interdependence definitions (14393-14410), decoupling gloss (14601-14606), Thomas situations from Table 14.1 (21195-21240; the deep calls it Exhibit 14.4).
